passage: The youth centre in Leeds held a pizza night every Friday, and Jamal went because his mum made him. He took the chair nearest the door, hood up, phone out even though there was no signal. Bilal and three others from his class were arguing about a football match a few metres away. Jamal knew the answer; he had watched the whole second half. He kept quiet. They don't want me in it anyway, he thought, and scrolled through nothing. Once Bilal glanced over. 'You alright, mate?' Jamal shrugged without looking up. Bilal turned back to the others. By half eight the group had drifted to the pool table, and Jamal sat alone with a cold slice. See, he told himself on the walk home. Nobody talks to me. He didn't think about the shrug.

qa.q: Where did Jamal sit at the pizza night?
qa.a: Jamal took the chair nearest the door, hood up, phone out even though there was no signal.

qa.q: What was Jamal thinking when he kept quiet about the football argument?
qa.a: He felt unwanted, thinking 'They don't want me in it anyway', so he expected to be unwelcome even though he knew the answer.

qa.q: At which moment could Jamal have changed how the night went, and how?
qa.a: When Bilal asked 'You alright, mate?', Jamal could have looked up and mentioned the second half he watched, which would have let him into the conversation.

qa.q: How might Bilal have read Jamal's hood, phone and shrug?
qa.a: To Bilal it probably looked as if Jamal wasn't interested in them, so leaving him alone seemed like the polite thing to do.

grounding: Shows a teenager who expects classmates to reject him acting withdrawn, so they leave him alone and he takes that as proof.

passage: Room 14 of the Class 10 boys' hostel had cake for Mridul's birthday at nine, after study hour. Eshaan came because the warden said everyone should. He stood by the window, arms folded, and checked his watch twice where people could see. Last term someone had laughed at his accent in the mess; since then he had been sure the whole floor thought he was odd. When the carrom board came out, Mridul held a striker toward him. 'Play one round?' 'I'm okay,' Eshaan said, and yawned, though he wasn't tired. Mridul passed the striker on. Later, walking to brush his teeth, Eshaan heard Mridul in the corridor: 'Leave him, yaar, he finds us boring.' Eshaan lay in his bunk, face hot. Knew it, he thought. They never wanted me there.

qa.q: What did Mridul offer Eshaan when the carrom board came out?
qa.a: Mridul held a striker toward him and asked, 'Play one round?'

qa.q: Why did Eshaan's face go hot in his bunk?
qa.a: He felt hurt, and he took Mridul's words as proof of what he had believed since last term, that the floor thought he was odd.

qa.q: What choice at the carrom board might have changed the night for Eshaan?
qa.a: Taking the striker for just one round would have shown the others he wanted to be there, instead of the folded arms and yawn they read as boredom.

qa.q: Why might Mridul have said 'he finds us boring'?
qa.a: From where Mridul stood, Eshaan checked his watch, yawned and turned down the game, so it honestly looked like Eshaan didn't want their company.

grounding: Illustrates how a boy's belief that his hostel mates dislike him leads to cold behaviour that makes them step back, which he reads as confirmation.

passage:
Dear Sangeeta akka,
You asked how the new school is. Same as I said. The girls here have known each other since KG and they don't want a new girl in the group.
Last Saturday there was a class picnic at the lake. I sat on the steps with my book and my earphones in. No music. I just didn't want anyone thinking I was waiting to be asked.
Two girls did come over and said the samosas were in the blue box. I said 'okay' and went back to reading. After that they didn't come again. On the bus home I sat alone.
Amma says I should 'make an effort'. What effort, when they've already decided?
Maybe I look like I don't care. I do care, a bit. Don't tell Amma that part.
Love,
Lakshmi

qa.q: What did the two girls tell Lakshmi at the picnic?
qa.a: They said the samosas were in the blue box.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi wear earphones with no music at the picnic?
qa.a: Lakshmi didn't want anyone thinking Lakshmi was waiting to be asked, which suggests a fear of looking hopeful and then being turned away.

qa.q: When the two girls came over, what could Lakshmi have done differently?
qa.a: Lakshmi could have taken the earphones out, thanked them and walked to the blue box with them, giving the conversation a chance to keep going.

qa.q: How might the two girls have felt after Lakshmi said 'okay' and went back to the book?
qa.a: They probably felt brushed off and decided Lakshmi preferred to be alone, which is why they didn't come again.

grounding: Shows a teenage girl who assumes the classmates don't want a newcomer, stays closed off at a picnic, and then sees their distance as proof.

passage: You want to know why I was such a wall on the museum trip, Sunaina? Okay. I'm Zainab, and I'd decided before the bus even came that nobody in 10C liked me. New school, new city, everyone already in pairs. So I got on first, took the window, put my earphones in with nothing playing, and stared at the flyover like it was fascinating. When you asked if the seat was free, I said "whatever" without looking up. You sat somewhere else. At the museum I trailed at the back and yawned, loudly, to show I didn't care. By lunch nobody was even trying. And I thought, see? Told you. It took me till March, when you said you'd all thought I hated you, to realise I'd written the whole story myself and then acted it out.

qa.q: What did Zainab say when Sunaina asked if the seat was free?
qa.a: "Whatever", without looking up.

qa.q: How did Zainab feel before the bus came, and how did that shape the day?
qa.a: Zainab felt lonely and sure nobody in 10C liked the new student, so the silent earphones, the yawns and the 'whatever' all came from expecting rejection.

qa.q: Where was the turning point on the bus, and what could Zainab have done instead?
qa.a: When Sunaina asked about the seat, Zainab could have taken the earphones out and said "yes, sit", a small risk that might have changed the whole trip.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt when Zainab said 'whatever' without looking up?
qa.a: Sunaina probably felt brushed off and unwelcome, sat somewhere else, and, like the rest of 10C, came to think Zainab hated them.

grounding: A new student expects classmates to dislike them, acts bored and distant on a trip, and the class's withdrawal seems to prove the belief.

passage: I'm Farida, and I've played on the colony basketball team for two years. Rehana joined in July. From day one she sat at the far end of the bench, scrolling, and when we did the circle chant before games she stood a step outside it with her arms folded. If someone passed her the ball in warm-ups, she passed it straight back without a word. After a couple of weeks people stopped passing to her. Stopped asking if she wanted chai after practice, too. Last Sunday I heard her tell her brother at the gate, "Told you. They don't want me there." I nearly laughed, because we'd all decided she didn't want us. I can't know what's going on in her head. But on Tuesday I'm going to sit at the far end of the bench and see what happens.

qa.q: Where did Rehana sit from day one?
qa.a: At the far end of the bench, scrolling.

qa.q: What does Rehana's "Told you. They don't want me there" suggest she expected all along?
qa.a: It suggests she felt rejected from the start and took the team's pulling back as proof, without seeing that her own distance had helped cause it.

qa.q: What is Farida's plan for Tuesday, and why might it break the loop?
qa.a: Farida plans to sit at Rehana's end of the bench; one friendly move could give Rehana different evidence from the story she expected.

qa.q: How had the team read Rehana's folded arms and silence?
qa.a: The team decided Rehana didn't want them, so they stopped passing and inviting, each side reading the other as the one who wasn't interested.

grounding: A teammate watches a new player who seems to expect rejection hold herself apart, so the others pull back, which she takes as proof.
